advances: Uniform planar area and finitely many proper chords individually bisected at a common point, with a balance of their oriented endpoints. No construction of such chords in an arbitrary mixed-integer cover and no higher-dimensional stationary-section estimate.

proof:
For each $i$, $K\cap\mathbb R p_i=[-p_i,p_i]$, because $0$ is interior and each ray from $0$ meets $\partial K$ at a unique point. Conversely, a proper chord with midpoint $0$ and length $S_i$ whose cap has inward unit normal $u_i$ has the signed endpoint $p_i=-R(u_i)S_i/2$. Then $Rp_i=S_i u_i/2$, so the balance in the statement is equivalent to $\sum_i\theta_i S_i u_i=0$. For through-point cap areas $y\mapsto |K\cap\{x:u_i\cdot(x-y)\ge0\}|$, the gradient at $0$ is $-S_i u_i$. Indeed, integration in the normal coordinate gives the derivative of area with respect to the threshold as minus the section length, which is continuous at an interior threshold by concavity of the planar section length. For the unnormalized normal $Rp_i$, the section-length factor per unit threshold is $S_i/\lVert Rp_i\rVert=2$.

**Reduction to two or three chords.** The feasible weights form a compact polytope. At an extreme weight vector the columns $(1,p_i)$ of its positive support are independent, since a nonzero dependence yields a small feasible variation in both signs. The cap mean is linear in the weights, and every feasible weight vector is a convex combination of extreme ones. It suffices to consider each extreme support. One point cannot balance, two points must lie on opposite rays, and independence excludes a collinear triple. For a pair, uniqueness of the radial boundary points gives $p_2=-p_1$ and $\theta_1=\theta_2=1/2$. The caps are complementary up to an area-null line, giving mean $|K|/2$.

For a positive noncollinear triple, each $\theta_i\le1/2$. If $\theta_i>1/2$, the equation $\theta_i p_i=\sum_{j\ne i}\theta_j(-p_j)$ puts $p_i$ in a convex combination with positive weight at the interior point $0$, a contradiction. If $\theta_3=1/2$, the same equation makes $p_3$ an interior point of the segment $[-p_1,-p_2]$, and $-p_3$ lies in the relative interior of $[p_1,p_2]$. A supporting line at either of these relative interior points contains the corresponding segment. Thus in coordinates $x=a p_1+b p_2$ the body $K$ lies in $|a+b|\le1$. Put $H=\operatorname{conv}\{\pm p_1,\pm p_2\}$, given by $|a|+|b|\le1$. For $x\in K\setminus H$, $a$ and $b$ have opposite signs. Hence $\det(p_1,x)$ and $\det(p_2,x)$ have the same strict sign, and $\det(p_3,x)$ has the opposite sign by balance. The weighted indicator $W(x)=\sum_i\theta_i\mathbf1_{H_i}(x)$ is $1/2$ there. Its integral over $H$ is $|H|/2$ by symmetry, since $W(x)+W(-x)=1$ off the three lines. This gives exactly $|K|/2$ for the half-weight case.

**Reduction to a triangle.** Suppose all three weights are strictly less than $1/2$. Relabel the triple and apply an orientation-preserving invertible linear map to take $p_1=(1,0)$, $p_2=(0,1)$, $p_3=(-a,-b)$ with $a,b>0$. The orientation condition preserves signs of $\det(p_i,x)=(Rp_i)\cdot x$, and the map multiplies all areas by one factor. The strict weight conditions say $a+b>1$, $1+b>a$, and $1+a>b$. In cyclic order the six marks are $(1,0),(a,b),(0,1),(-1,0),(-a,-b),(0,-1)$. They lie on the boundary of their convex hull $H$ because they are on $\partial K$, and $0$ is interior to $H$. In this angular order the first three successive turns have determinants $1+b-a$, $a+b-1$, and $1+a-b$, and the opposite three repeat them. Thus $H$ is a strictly convex hexagon in the sense that every mark is a vertex. The values of $W$ in the sectors between these rays alternate between a singleton weight $\theta_i$ and a sum $1-\theta_i>1/2$. This also follows from the positive dependence: away from the lines there are either one or two positive signs, and crossing one line changes exactly one sign.

For each sector of weight greater than $1/2$, cut $K$ with the halfplane through the sector's two boundary marks that contains $0$. The halfplane contains $H$. If its line supports $K$, nothing is removed. Otherwise $K$ meets the line precisely in the segment between the two marks. To see this, a point of $\partial K$ in the relative interior of a line section forces any supporting line there to contain that section, so the section line would support $K$. Write the cutting line as $f(x)=1$ with $f$ linear. Any removed point $x$ satisfies $f(x)>1$ and has $x/f(x)$ in the line section, so it lies in the sector of its two marks, up to boundary rays. Let $K'$ be the intersection after all three cuts. Then $H\subseteq K'$ and
$$
\int_K(W-4/9)\ge \int_{K'}(W-4/9),
$$
with strict inequality if a positive area was removed.

The three retained halfplanes define a bounded triangle $T$. In the chosen coordinates their outward normals can be taken as $(b,1-a)$, $(-1,1)$, $(b-1,-a)$ with right sides $b,1,a$. They span the plane and have positive dependence with coefficients $1+a-b$, $a+b-1$, $1+b-a$, so they have no nonzero common recession direction. Their lines support three distinct edges of $H$, and $0$ satisfies all three inequalities strictly. Their reflections support the other three edges. Consequently $H\subseteq K'\subseteq T$ and $H=T\cap(-T)$.

**Corner areas and weights.** Let $v_0,v_1,v_2$ be the vertices of $T$ in counterclockwise order, $l_i$ the barycentric coordinates of $0$, and $\lambda_i(x)$ those of a variable point. In $T$ the constraints from $-T$ are $\lambda_i(x)\le2l_i$, since $\lambda_i(-x)=2l_i-\lambda_i(x)$. Each inequality supplies an edge of the hexagon, so $0<l_i<1/2$. Set $t_i=1-2l_i$ and $e=\sum_{i<j}t_i t_j$. Then $t_i>0$, $\sum_i t_i=1$, and $e>0$. The disjoint corners $Q_i=\{x\in T:\lambda_i(x)>1-t_i\}$ have area $t_i^2|T|$, by linear scaling about $v_i$. They are disjoint because $(1-t_i)+(1-t_j)>1$ for distinct $i,j$. The section of $T$ along each reflected edge line is exactly the segment between its two marked vertices, so the same radial argument puts $Q_i$ in the corresponding singleton sector. Thus $|H|=(1-\sum_i t_i^2)|T|=2e|T|$.

For cyclic $(i,j,k)$ put $q_i=t_kv_i+(1-t_k)v_k$. These are marked endpoints, at $\lambda_j=0$ and $\lambda_k=1-t_k$. Their antipodes are $-q_i=t_j v_i+(1-t_j)v_j$, as follows from $2\sum_i l_i v_i=0$. The six points give all marked endpoints because these are precisely the intersections of a side of $T$ with an adjacent reflected constraint. The cap oriented by $Rq_i$ contains $v_i$ and misses $v_j,v_k$. Indeed $\det(v_j,v_k)=2|T|l_i$ in cyclic order, and
$$
(\det(q_i,v_i),\det(q_i,v_j),\det(q_i,v_k))
=|T|\big((1-t_k)(1-t_j),-(1-t_k)t_j,-t_k(1-t_j)\big).
$$
The weights $\beta_i=t_i(1-t_i)/(2e)$ sum to one and balance the $q_i$. The coefficient of $v_i$ in $\sum_h\beta_h q_h$ is
$$
\frac{t_i(1-t_i)t_k+t_j(1-t_j)(1-t_i)}{2e}
=\frac{1-t_i}{2}=l_i.
$$
These three directions are distinct and span the plane, so their space of relations is one-dimensional. The original balanced triple, after permuting it to correspond to the $q_i$, must choose either all $q_i$ or all $-q_i$, since it also has a positive dependence. Reversing all three would make every corner lie in two caps, whereas each lies in a singleton sector. Thus the original orientation is $q_i$, the weights are $\theta_i=\beta_i$, and $W=\theta_i$ on $Q_i$ off the lines.

The integral of $W$ on $H$ is $|H|/2$. Writing $a_i=|K'\cap Q_i|/|T|$, the normalized integral of $W-4/9$ on $K'$ is the affine function
$$
\frac1{|T|}\int_{K'}(W-4/9)=\frac{e}{9}+\sum_i(\theta_i-4/9)a_i.
$$
Each $a_i\in[0,t_i^2]$. It suffices to test the eight box vertices, since every point in the box is a convex combination of them. For the vertex with $a_i=t_i^2$ on $I$ and zero elsewhere, multiply the affine function by $18e>0$. Its value is
$$
E_I=2e^2+\sum_{i\in I}t_i^2\bigl(9t_i(1-t_i)-8e\bigr).
$$

**The eight vertices.** For $I=\varnothing$ the value is positive. For $I=\{0,1,2\}$ set $f=t_0t_1t_2$. From $\sum_i t_i=1$ one has $\sum_i t_i^2=1-2e$ and $\sum_i(t_i^3-t_i^4)=e-2e^2-f$. Substitution gives $E_I=e-9f=f(\sum_i1/t_i-9)\ge0$ by Cauchy–Schwarz, with equality precisely when all $t_i=1/3$.

For a singleton let $t$ be the included coordinate, $s=1-t$, and $v$ the product of the other two. Then $0<v\le s^2/4$ and $e=ts+v$. Expansion gives
$$
E_I=2(v+ts-2t^2)^2+t^3(9-17t).
$$
This is strictly positive for $t\le1/2$. For $t\ge1/2$ its derivative in $v$ is $4(v+t-3t^2)\le 1+2t-11t^2<0$ on this interval of $v$. At $v=s^2/4$ it equals $s(1+5t-13t^2+15t^3)/8>0$. The bracket starts at one and has everywhere positive derivative $45t^2-26t+5$, whose discriminant is negative.

For two included indices let $t$ be the omitted coordinate, $s=1-t$, and $v$ the product of the included coordinates. Substituting $e=ts+v$ gives
$$
E_I=s\bigl[ts(1+t)+(1-8t)v\bigr].
$$
For $t\le1/8$ this is positive. For $t>1/8$, the upper bound $v\le s^2/4$ gives $E_I\ge s^2(1-5t+12t^2)/4>0$, since the quadratic has negative discriminant and positive leading coefficient. The box inequality and the truncation inequality give the desired cap bound.

**Equality.** In a strict triple equality forces $t_0=t_1=t_2=1/3$ and every corner filled, since the all-corners vertex is then the only zero of the affine function among the box vertices. It also forces the deleted area to be zero. Hence $K'=T$ and $K=K'$. Here we use that if one convex body properly contains another, a point outside the smaller one can be moved slightly toward an interior point of the larger one to obtain an open ball in their difference. Since $l_i=1/3$, $0$ is the centroid. The endpoints of the $i$-th chord both have $\lambda_i=1/3$ and the cap contains $v_i$, so these are the stated vertex caps, and the weights are $1/3$. Conversely, for a triangle centered at its centroid, the facet-parallel vertex caps have bisected chords, their three signed endpoints balance with weights $1/3$ by the formulas above, and each cap has area $(2/3)^2|K|$. Finally, equality for an arbitrary weight vector forces equality in each extreme weight vector used with positive coefficient in its convex decomposition. Every such extreme vector uses the same three canonical caps of the triangle and assigns weight $1/3$ to each. A cap orientation determines its signed endpoint uniquely. This proves the classification after repeated orientations are merged.

statement:
Let $K\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a compact convex body with $0\in\operatorname{int}K$. Let $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ be nonzero vectors with $p_i,-p_i\in\partial K$ for every $i$. Write $R(x_1,x_2)=(-x_2,x_1)$ and $H_i=\{x:(Rp_i)\cdot x\ge0\}$. If $\theta_i\ge0$, $\sum_i\theta_i=1$, and $\sum_i\theta_i p_i=0$, then
$$
\sum_i\theta_i|K\cap H_i|\ge \frac49|K|,
$$
where $|\cdot|$ denotes planar area. The constant is sharp. Equality holds exactly when $K$ is a triangle with centroid $0$ and, after dropping zero weights and merging repeated oriented chords, the three $H_i$ are the vertex halfplanes through $0$ parallel to the opposite sides, with total weight $1/3$ on each. A balanced opposite pair, or a positive noncollinear triple with one weight $1/2$, has weighted cap area $|K|/2$.
title: Sharp weighted area bound for bisected planar chords
